assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collateral constraints and credit-cycle amplification are a foundational mechanism in macro-finance. Kiyotaki-Moore's model of how asset prices and borrowing limits reinforce each other, together with Gertler's financial-accelerator and intermediary work, shaped how economists and central banks understood the 2008 crisis and policy responses. The work is theory-led and has also been applied to policy and empirical research.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore have the clearest claim, through their 1997 credit-cycles paper. Gertler's contributions (financial accelerator with Bernanke, later intermediary models) are central, but the Bernanke link is complicated by his 2022 prize. Gilchrist's empirical contributions are real but more derivative, so I keep the trio to three.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The core papers date from the 1990s, and the framework has been tested and extended through the 2008 crisis and later work. The 2022 prize on banks and financial crises makes this a related, not duplicative, recognition.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises could count against it.
Whether Gertler or Gilchrist should be in the trio instead of or alongside Kiyotaki and Moore.
I have not independently verified citation or influence metrics.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Law and finance opened a major empirical research program on how legal institutions and investor protection shape financial development, ownership structure and growth. It changed corporate finance, comparative institutions and development policy, and it links closely to work on contracting and governance.
assessment.attribution: The LLSV collaboration is tightly integrated, and Shleifer is the intellectual center, also through his wider behavioral-finance and corporate-governance work. Vishny is a core co-author on governance papers, but the legal-origins agenda is mainly La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes and Shleifer. The three-name limit forces a choice.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with foundational papers from 1997-2008 and about three decades of follow-up and replication.
uncertainties: Legal-origins causal claims and the coding of legal variables have been seriously criticized, which could weaken the scientific case.
Reputational controversy around Shleifer could affect committee views.
Whether Vishny's omission is defensible.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework, built on nominal rigidities, policy rules and a micro-founded monetary theory, is the standard for monetary policy analysis in central banks. Its influence on practice and teaching is very large.
assessment.attribution: Attribution is the main difficulty, since the contributions are diffuse: Calvo (staggered pricing), Taylor (staggered contracts and the policy rule), Woodford (synthesis and optimal policy), Gali, Christiano-Eichenbaum and Smets (estimated DSGE models). Calvo, Taylor and Woodford capture foundations, rule and synthesis, but any trio leaves out important contributors.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with 1980s-2000s foundations and decades of practical use. Its performance during and after the 2008 crisis and the 2021-22 inflation episode is debated.
uncertainties: Many strong contributors, so any selection is contestable.
Mixed empirical and policy performance in recent crises.
Overlap with earlier macro prizes on rational expectations and monetary policy.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection transformed trade theory and empirics, adding the extensive margin, reallocation gains and exporter premia that the new trade theory (2008 prize) did not capture. It is a major, widely adopted framework with clear empirical grounding.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the clear core. Helpman's contributions (Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exports versus FDI, plus earlier trade theory) are substantial. Redding is a strong later contributor, but the pair captures the central credit.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The key 2003-2004 papers have decades of follow-up, and the framework is now standard in trade.
uncertainties: Krugman's 2008 prize partly overlaps in subject, and Helpman's other work (political-economy trade, growth) may be competing recognition in B030.
Whether Redding or Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum deserve credit for related parallel work (the latter not on this ballot).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the China-shock evidence reshaped understanding of labor-market polarization, wage inequality and regional adjustment to trade. The work has had large effects on research and on political and policy debate.
assessment.attribution: Autor is the central figure across the task and trade-shock strands. Hanson and Dorn are essential on the China-shock papers. Katz has a long record on skill-biased change and inequality but is also credited under B045, and the task framework has theoretical contributors (Acemoglu, Autor) outside this ballot.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature. The task framework dates from the early 2000s and the China-shock papers from 2013-2016, and some conclusions (persistence, magnitudes) are still debated.
uncertainties: Measurement and identification debates over the China shock.
Acemoglu's role in the task framework is not credited in this entry.
Whether the empirical contribution is seen as separable from the theory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Partial identification systematically asks what can be learned from data under weak assumptions, and it underpins credible inference in applied work, from treatment effects to structural models. It is a genuine conceptual contribution to econometric methodology.
assessment.attribution: Manski is the clear founder (bounds from the late 1980s onward). Tamer is the leading figure in moment-inequality and incomplete-model econometrics. Molinari is a major contributor but a younger one, so the pair is the most defensible core.
assessment.maturity: Mature in concept, with a 35-year record. Practical adoption is real but narrower than the identification-credibility revolution recognized in 2021.
uncertainties: Applied uptake is narrower than for design-based methods.
Methodological prizes need a strong case for broad impact on empirical practice.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Top-income and wealth-distribution series built from tax data created a new empirical basis for studying inequality and put distribution at the center of economics and policy. The data infrastructure (World Inequality Database) has had a large influence.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are the originators of the long-run top-income series. Zucman extends the work to wealth and offshore holdings. The contribution is mostly measurement and data construction, with limited causal or theoretical identification.
assessment.maturity: Reasonably mature. The 2003 Piketty-Saez series is two decades old, but the wealth and offshore estimates are more recent and still debated.
uncertainties: Methodological critiques of the distributional national accounts and the wealth-capitalization estimates.
Whether measurement without sharp causal claims is judged sufficient.
Policy advocacy by the candidates may complicate perceptions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Machine learning for causal inference (double/debiased ML, causal forests, heterogeneous treatment effects) is a methodological advance with fast uptake in empirical economics. Athey also has distinct, wide-ranging contributions in industrial organization and market design.
assessment.attribution: Chernozhukov's double/debiased ML and Athey's causal-forest and heterogeneous-effects work are the two core strands. Wager is a key coauthor on forests, but the pair is the most defensible core. Athey also appears elsewhere (B024), which could split support.
assessment.maturity: Less mature. The main contributions date from roughly 2016-2018, so the long-run impact on scientific practice is still unfolding.
uncertainties: Timing: the committee may prefer more time to judge lasting influence.
Credit-splitting among many contributors to ML-based causal methods, including those outside the ballot.
Chernozhukov also appears under B038 for quantile regression.
